newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Sept 23.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Sept 23.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- MORGAN GRENFELL TO CALL IN SFO OVER YOUNG DEALS

Following the internal investigation into the personal dealings of fund manager Peter Young, Morgan Grenfell is to call in the Serious Fraud Office. The move comes after the release of documents held in Switzerland by Juerg Wyler and Marco Wolf, Zurich-based lawyers, which include the day-to-day profit and loss accounts for six Luxembourg-listed holding companies set up by Mr Young to hold unlisted equities. Morgan Grenfell seized control of these holding companies the day it froze Mr Young's assets and is now concentrating on the flow of transactions between holding companies and examining any evidence of transactions with off-shore banking centres.
-- MAXWELL TEAM TAKES FIRM LINE WITH DTI MEN

Keith Oliver of law firm Peters and Peters, one of the lawyers representing Kevin Maxwell, gave notice that he will conduct a vigorous fight to prevent an inquiry that will cover old ground. Last week Mr Maxwell was cleared of a second fraud trial but still faces an investigation from inspectors appointed by the DTI. The lawyers say that Mr Maxwell will not appear before the DTI inspectors to discuss things already covered in the trial.
-- FORMER BARINGS MANAGER TO SUE FT

The former head of financial products at Barings, Ron Baker, has launched libel proceedings against the Financial Times and two of its journalists following the publication of articles which he calls "defamatory". The articles were based on extracts from a book called All That Glitters, by FT journalists John Gapper and Nicholas Denton, which chronicles the collapse of Barings. Mr Baker claims the articles imply that he contributed to the merchant bank's collapse because he was the immediate boss of Nick Leeson.
THE TIMES
-- FORMER RAIL DIRECTOR PAID FOUR MILLION STG FOR EIGHT DAYS' WORK

Peter Watson, a former British Rail director has received a four million stg profit for just eight days' work as non- executive chairman of the Porterbrook train leasing company. Shadow Transport Secretary Andrew Smith said the windfall exposed Government hypocracy over pledges to curb "fat cat" excesses during the rail sell-off.
-- CLARKE LOOKS TO DEFY GEORGE ON RATE INCREASE

There is growing evidence that Chancellor Kenneth Clarke will resist a call from the Governor of the Bank of England, Eddie George, for higher interest rates. This will widen the rift between the Treasury and the Bank over monetary policy. Evidence that the consumer side of the economy is strengthening rules out a further cut in interest rates. The markets also believe that Mr Clarke will continue to refuse to raise rates before the election.
-- NORWICH DECIDES ON FOUR BILLION STG FLOTATION

Norwich Union, the UK's second biggest mutual insurance company, is set to float on the Stock Exchange next summer and give bonuses averaging 700 stg to its three million with-profit policyholders. Policyholders must vote at a meeting in the spring on the conversion. The flotation will value the insurer at around four billion stg and will allow Norwich Union to raise extra capital to take part in the widespread consolidation in the financial services industry.
THE GUARDIAN
-- OFGAS INQUIRY INTO 'PRICE FIXING'

Ofgas has decided to investigate whether British Gas is forcing up the price of gas by restricting supplies. The director-general of gas supply, Clare Spottiswoode, is scrutinising whether British Gas is deliberately cutting production at its Morecambe Bay gas field in an attempt to push up wholesale gas prices. British Gas claims the Morecambe Bay was off-line for maintenance work to its offshore process equipment.
-- EXCHANGE SEEKS TO RAISE POLICING PROFILE

Senior executives at the Stock Exchange are pressing the Government for the right to publish the findings of its insider- dealing inquiries, in an effort to curb the failure of criminal prosecutors to secure convictions. They are unhappy with the burden of proof needed to nail the perpetrators of insider dealing and want to reveal details of their investigations. It is understood that the DTI is refusing to allow the Exchange to take matters into its own hands.
-- MIXED FORTUNES IN CONSTRUCTION

Improved profits from Barratt Developments and setbacks at Tarmac, Redland and Beazer Homes illustrates the varied fortunes of housebuilders and construction companies. Barratt plumbed greater depths during the recession than Beazer Homes but its rebound should push profits up seven percent. Tarmac's interims will be depressed by the housebuilding division it has sold to Wimpey and profits will be halved. Redland have suffered from bad weather at the start of the year and very weak markets.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- TOUR OPERATORS AGREE ON PACKAGE TO ESCAPE MMC

The Office of Fair Trading is set to reach an agreement over concessions from Britain's leading package tour operators that will allow them to escape a Monopolies and Mergers Commission reference into the holiday industry. Airtours and Thomson are prepared to sanction changes to the way they operate their travel agent subsidiaries in order to avoid a further probe. This is the second time in the last two years that the government has looked into the issues surrounding the "vertical integration" of the holiday business.
-- LLOYD'S PAYS 400,000 STG FOR HARD WORK

Lloyd's of London has defended the decision to award a 400,000 stg bonus to chairman David Rowland on the grounds that the money was in recognition of his efforts to push through the insurance market's 3.2 billion stg reconstruction package. The award comes on top of Mr Rowland's 450,000 stg salary package. The bonus is one of several being made to senior executives, including Ron Sandler. All awards will be paid by the market's central funds.
-- IMF WILL SELL GOLD RESERVES TO REDUCE DEBT IN THIRD WORLD

Plans are set to be put at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund in Washington next week to reduce the debt burden on the world's poorest countries. The proposal to sell part of the IMF's gold reserves and reinvest the proceeds was nearly derailed by German opposition. The fund's managing director Michel Camdessus announced last week that it would be able to finance its share of the debt relief plan. Senior officials believe the IMF can use alternative reserves for the next two years, after which it will sell a smaller part of its gold.
